items.text: MCP servers are independent: one that is offline does not stop the session from starting with the others. For a remote (HTTP/SSE) server, Claude Code retries a failed first connection up to three times on transient errors and then marks the server as failed; a stdio server is marked failed without those retries. Its tools are then missing, or calls return errors if the server drops later. Claude does not substitute tools from other servers (C), and a server that failed at startup is not polled until it comes back (D): in an interactive session you bring it back with Reconnect in `/mcp` (or `/mcp reconnect all`). Remote servers that drop mid-session are reconnected automatically up to five times with exponential backoff. Agents should still handle missing tools gracefully, especially for servers with maintenance windows.

Claude Code does not swap in built-in tools with matching names (A), calls don't keep running into 503 errors because the tools are simply absent (B), and there is no documented fixed-interval polling that loads the tools later (C).

items.text: Determinism has to come from pinning and validation, not from sampling settings: API version 2026-10-21 removes `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` (a request that sends any of them gets a 400 error on every model), and newer models reject them anyway. Generating twice (B) catches some non-determinism but does not stabilize the model or the output format.

items.text: Structured error metadata lets the agent react sensibly. `isError: true` marks the tool result as a failure, `errorCategory: "permission"` says it is an authorization problem, and `isRetryable: false` says retrying is pointless. Without that, the agent treats every error as possibly transient and retries in vain, delaying the user's awareness of an access issue. MCP reports tool execution errors inside the tool result, not through HTTP status codes (C); length alone does not make an error actionable (A); and auto-requesting elevated permissions (D) is a security anti-pattern. Note: `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable sind Konvention, kein MCP-Feld; HTTP-Aussage praezisiert.

items.text: The `isRetryable` flag exists precisely to differentiate these cases. "Required field missing" is input-validation retryable — the agent may be able to gather the missing data and re-invoke. "Business rule violation" is not retryable by the agent — it requires human intervention or policy change. Using `errorSubCategory` or additional descriptive fields to distinguish sub-types of validation errors, paired with correct `isRetryable` values, enables precise agent behavior. MCP reports tool execution errors inside the tool result, not through HTTP status codes; using "permission" for business rules is semantically incorrect. Note: `errorCategory`, `errorSubCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable/errorSubCategory sind Konvention, kein MCP-Feld; HTTP-Aussage praezisiert.

items.text: 503 errors represent temporary service unavailability — they are canonical transient errors. `errorCategory: "transient"` combined with `isRetryable: true` signals to the agent that retrying with exponential backoff is appropriate. `errorCategory: "business"` is for application logic failures that won't resolve without data or process changes; `"permission"` is for authorization failures. Returning false success with empty data corrupts the agent's understanding of actual results and prevents appropriate retry logic. Note: `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable sind eine Konvention aus dem Exam Guide, kein Feld der MCP-Spezifikation.

items.text: `isRetryable` is metadata for the consuming agent's recovery logic. `true` means the same call might succeed on retry (transient issues like network timeout). `false` means no amount of retrying will fix the issue (validation error, policy violation) — the agent should take a different action instead. Note: `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable sind eine Konvention aus dem Exam Guide, kein Feld der MCP-Spezifikation.

items.text: Permission errors are non-retryable because the underlying issue (account tier, authorization level) won't change between API calls. The agent should communicate the specific limitation to the user with the information needed to resolve it (upgrade subscription) rather than retrying or attempting workarounds. Note: `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable sind eine Konvention aus dem Exam Guide, kein Feld der MCP-Spezifikation.

items.text: `errorCategory` enables category-based recovery logic: transient → retry, validation → ask user for corrected input, permission → explain limitation and escalate, business → communicate policy to user. Without categories, agents must either parse error messages (brittle) or apply a single recovery strategy to all errors (inefficient). Note: `errorCategory` and `isRetryable` are not fields of the MCP specification, which only marks a failed tool call with `isError: true` in the tool result; they are a structured-error convention (used in the exam guide) that the server puts into the error content.
items.why: Klarstellung: errorCategory/isRetryable sind eine Konvention aus dem Exam Guide, kein Feld der MCP-Spezifikation.

items.text: Prompt caching matches prefixes: a cache hit needs the prompt to be identical up to the cached breakpoint, so editing CLAUDE.md invalidates the cached prefix from that point on, including the code examples and instructions behind it. The next request writes the new prefix to the cache (1.25x the base input price for the default 5-minute TTL), and later requests read it again at the much cheaper cache-read rate. The impact is therefore a one-off write per change, and batching convention edits keeps those writes rare. There is no partial re-caching of only the changed section (A), CLAUDE.md content in the cached prefix is cached like any other prompt content (B), and a cache entry is not updated in place (C).
items.why: Erklaerung an Caching-Doku angepasst (einmaliger Cache-Write, danach wieder Treffer).

items.text: `--resume` (or `resume` in the Agent SDK) reopens a saved session and keeps adding to that same history. Forking (`--fork-session`, or `fork_session` together with `resume` in the SDK) creates a new session that starts with a copy of the history, while the original's ID and history stay unchanged, so you can return to the state before the branch. Neither is deprecated, and speed or usage limits are not the difference. Forking branches the conversation, not the outside world: it cannot undo a funds transfer or any other external side effect, and not even file changes. A real rollback needs transactional safeguards in the systems themselves.

items.text: Replacing the generic tool with a purpose-specific one makes the restriction part of the tool's contract: `load_document` validates every URL against the approved list before fetching, whatever the prompt says. A system-prompt rule (A) is only an instruction the model may not follow. items.text: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop is the reliability pattern the guide describes. Strict tool use (`strict: true`) or Structured Outputs guarantee the schema; validation then catches semantic errors, and retrying with the error fed back fixes most of them. Reviewing every record (A) does not scale, majority voting (B) triples cost without checking anything, and temperature zero (D) accepts unchecked output; API version 2026-10-21 also removes `temperature` entirely (400 on every model).
